title: Employee Transfer

jokes.text: Stanley is dressed as Urkel / wearing glasses so he can sleep at his desk without being noticed
jokes.setup: Someone asks why Stanley, who hates Halloween, is dressed up in a costume
jokes.punchline: He's wearing it so he can sleep at his desk — the costume is purely functional, not festive
jokes.explanation: Perfectly character-integrated — Stanley's laziness and hatred of performative fun is a core trait, and this subverts the Halloween costume premise brilliantly. The punchline recontextualizes the costume as a sleep aid, which is both absurd and completely in character. Strong craft.

jokes.text: Kevin dressed as Carrie Bradshaw from Sex and the City, saying 'I like your shoes' and asking to be walked to the fax machine
jokes.setup: Someone asks Kevin who he is; Kevin, a large man, announces he's Carrie Bradshaw from Sex and the City
jokes.punchline: He then asks to be walked to the fax machine, leaning into the bit with a delighted sincerity
jokes.explanation: The visual of Kevin in a Carrie Bradshaw costume is inherently funny, but the extra beat of asking to be 'walked to the fax machine' elevates it — he's fully committed and earnest, which is peak Kevin comedy.

jokes.text: Michael dressed as Gordon Gekko; someone mistakes him for someone from 'the insurance commercials'
jokes.setup: Michael asks 'Who are you, Larry King?' implying he thinks his own costume is obscure; someone asks who he is and he says 'Gordon Gekko'
jokes.punchline: The other person responds: 'From the insurance commercials.' — a deflating misidentification that wounds Michael's ego
jokes.explanation: A solid deflation joke — Michael thinks he's cultured and clever, and someone flattens him by connecting his costume to GEICO geckos. Competent and character-appropriate, though not exceptional.

jokes.text: Someone (likely Dwight) in a Joker costume says 'Let's put a smile on that face'
jokes.setup: The office Halloween scene; someone enters with an elaborate costume
jokes.punchline: A deadpan delivery of the Joker's catchphrase — the humor is in Dwight's total commitment to character, which is itself in character for Dwight
jokes.explanation: A reference joke that works because Dwight's intensity fits the Joker's menace. Not particularly original — it's essentially just quoting a movie — but the character match is strong.

jokes.text: 'Damn it, Creed. I've been up since 4:00.'
jokes.setup: Creed appears in a costume (implied to be something deeply unsettling, like a bloody or disturbing outfit); someone reacts with alarm
jokes.punchline: Creed deflects all concern about the costume's disturbing nature by mentioning he's been up since 4am — implying he built the costume himself and is oblivious to how wrong it is
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. The joke works on multiple levels: Creed's response implies pride in effort rather than shame at the reaction, suggesting he has no idea (or no care) that his costume is disturbing. The '4:00' detail is perfectly specific and mundane against the presumably horrifying visual. Creed's entire comedic persona — the accidental menace, the disconnected sincerity — is distilled into two short lines. Earns the 8+ score.

jokes.text: Someone asks a person in a costume who they are; they say 'Dave.' 'Cool. And you are?' — implying they're not in a costume at all
jokes.setup: The office Halloween parade of costumes; someone compliments a 'sweet 'stume' and asks who the person is
jokes.punchline: 'Dave.' — the person is just dressed as themselves/wearing regular clothes, and the questioner treats it as a valid costume answer
jokes.explanation: A classic comedy beat — is Dave in a costume or not? The ambiguity is the joke. Good economy, but low character integration since 'Dave' is presumably a minor/background character.

jokes.text: Pam's art school friends dressed as cats; someone asks 'A cat?' and Pam corrects: 'We were looking for kitten.'
jokes.setup: Someone identifies Pam's art school friends' costumes as 'a cat'
jokes.punchline: 'We were looking for kitten' — Pam gently corrects the artistic vision that fell short of the execution
jokes.explanation: A mild observational joke about costume ambition vs. execution. Works as a small moment but isn't particularly memorable or character-specific.

jokes.text: Jim in New York — no one dresses up for Halloween at corporate; Jim is in full costume with greasepaint mustache
jokes.setup: Jim mentions his costume is getting a lot of attention at the New York corporate office
jokes.punchline: 'Apparently no one dresses up for Halloween here' — Jim has dressed up in an office culture that doesn't do that, now standing out embarrassingly
jokes.explanation: Good cringe setup — Jim, usually the cool one, is the awkward fool in a new environment. The role reversal is satisfying. But it's setup for the next joke rather than a complete bit on its own.

jokes.text: 'I wish I had known that before I used greasepaint for my mustache, and I can't even take off my hat because then I'm Hitler.'
jokes.setup: Jim is in costume with a greasepaint mustache at a corporate office that doesn't do Halloween; he can't easily remove the costume
jokes.punchline: Removing the hat reveals a Hitler-adjacent look — Jim is trapped in the costume because the hat is the only thing making it NOT Hitler
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The escalation is perfect — Jim explains he can't remove his hat because 'then I'm Hitler.' The economy is surgical: the mustache + hat = Charlie Chaplin/specific costume, but hat removed = Hitler. The logic is airtight, the stakes are absurd but real, and the delivery as a helpless confessional is perfectly in Jim's register. Highly quotable, visually funny even in audio form. Easily an 8+ joke — comparable in craft to the anchor examples.

jokes.text: Dwight (as Joker) performs a 'magic trick' to make a pencil disappear — visually mimicking the Joker's pencil scene from The Dark Knight
jokes.setup: Dwight in Joker costume announces he'll make a pencil disappear
jokes.punchline: The implied visual of Dwight slamming the pencil into a table (or someone's face) referencing the Dark Knight scene — the gap from [01:41] to [01:49] is the comedic pause before the 'trick'
jokes.explanation: The 8-second gap between the setup and 'disappear' is the comedic beat — Dwight commits fully to a violent movie reference in a workplace setting. Works well as a visual gag even described in text, and Dwight's intensity makes it character-appropriate.

jokes.text: Michael has packed puzzles, string for cat's cradles, puppets, and a road-trip CD for a 7-hour drive
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly are about to go on a road trip; Holly says 'Look at all this stuff. It's only seven hours.'
jokes.punchline: The inventory — puzzles, cat's cradle string, puppets — is absurdly childlike and over-prepared for a short drive; Michael treats it as perfectly normal
jokes.explanation: Michael's childlike enthusiasm for the road trip is perfectly in character. The escalating list (puzzles → string → puppets) builds nicely, and Holly's 'it's only seven hours' grounds it. Good character comedy.

jokes.text: Michael burned a 'road-trip CD' for the drive
jokes.setup: Michael mentions he burned a CD last night for the road trip
jokes.punchline: The CD is called a 'Little Road-Trip CD' — the mundane earnestness of it, combined with the rest of the over-prepared supplies, paints Michael as someone treating a 7-hour drive like a cross-country expedition
jokes.explanation: Supporting joke to the larger 'Michael over-prepares' bit. Functional but not particularly funny on its own.

jokes.text: 'Breaker 1-9, copy?' / 'Copy that, breaker! Those Duke boys are at it again.' / 'Hey, do not touch my radio.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly are on the road together; Michael grabs the CB radio voice
jokes.punchline: Holly plays along perfectly ('Those Duke boys are at it again'), then Michael snaps her back to reality when she touches his radio — the intimacy of the bit followed by a sudden possessiveness
jokes.explanation: The chemistry between Michael and Holly is the engine here. The Dukes of Hazzard reference is dated but fitting for Michael's cultural touchstones; Holly matching his energy is endearing. The sudden 'do not touch my radio' deflation is a nice comedic turn.

jokes.text: Holly's talking-head: The relationship dispute ended with Michael saying 'I asked you first,' then both saying 'first' simultaneously, then Michael saying 'Jinx' — and they never discussed who moves again
jokes.setup: Holly explains the unresolved question of who should quit their job and move
jokes.punchline: The adult relationship dilemma was resolved (or buried) by a children's 'jinx' game — neither party addressed it again
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best jokes in the episode. The escalation from a serious relationship decision to 'I asked you first' to both saying 'first' simultaneously to Michael invoking 'Jinx' is perfectly structured. Each step escalates the immaturity, and 'and then we never talked about it again' is a devastating deadpan kicker. Holly's bemused delivery implied by the confessional context makes it land harder. Earns 8+ easily.

jokes.text: Michael tells Jim he can let people go a couple minutes early if he wants
jokes.setup: Michael leaves Jim in charge and whispers a special directive
jokes.punchline: The 'perk' Michael bestows is letting people go a few minutes early — a trivial, not-actually-special power that Michael treats as a gift
jokes.explanation: Michael treating a minor privilege as a grand bestowal is in character. Functional joke, not particularly sharp.

jokes.text: Jim's talking-head: 'My brother Pete from Boston and my brother Tom from New Jersey are taking Pam and I out for lunch to celebrate the engagement. Or maybe to beat me up. I can never tell with those two.'
jokes.setup: Jim explains the lunch plan with his brothers to celebrate the engagement
jokes.punchline: 'Or maybe to beat me up. I can never tell with those two.' — the cheerful uncertainty about his brothers' intentions
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed talking head joke. The setup is grounded and realistic; the punchline subverts the celebratory framing with casual menace. 'I can never tell with those two' is the kicker that makes it land — Jim's fond acceptance of his brothers' aggression is character-specific and funny.

jokes.text: Dwight arrives in casual clothes (Cornell sweatshirt) — 'I thought I'd go casual today'
jokes.setup: Dwight, normally in his signature beet-farmer uniform, arrives in a Cornell sweatshirt
jokes.punchline: Dwight treating a college sweatshirt as 'going casual' is both funny for the visual and for what it signals — he's already scheming with the Cornell angle
jokes.explanation: A decent setup joke that pays off later in the Cornell subplot. Mild on its own but functions well as a plant.

jokes.text: Andy tells Dwight 'Take that sweatshirt off' as if it's a joke, then immediately is revealed to be serious
jokes.setup: Andy sees Dwight in a Cornell sweatshirt, laughs, and says 'That's funny. Take that sweatshirt off' — seemingly joking
jokes.punchline: The scene cut reveals Andy is completely serious about his Cornell pride and deeply threatened by Dwight wearing the colors
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — Andy's laugh signals a joke, but the pivot to genuine outrage is perfectly Andy. His college identity being his most precious possession is a well-established character trait.

jokes.text: Dwight says 'if someone who barely outsells Phyllis can get in, then I should be fine'
jokes.setup: Dwight explains why he thinks he can get into Cornell
jokes.punchline: Dwight insults Andy's academic caliber by comparing him to Phyllis (the implied weakest seller) — then backpedals by claiming it was a compliment to Phyllis AND a slight to Andy simultaneously
jokes.explanation: A layered joke with excellent structure. Dwight insults Andy through Phyllis (herself sitting right there), then immediately claims dual purpose — 'a compliment to you, Phyllis, as well as a slight to Andy.' The Phyllis inclusion ('I'm sitting right here') and Dwight's instant rationalization are both character-perfect. One of the tighter joke constructions in the episode.

jokes.text: Michael and Holly singing along to 'Life Is a Highway' at full volume during the road trip
jokes.setup: Michael announces he loves this song; the road-trip CD plays
jokes.punchline: Both fully commit to singing — the earnestness and joy of two dorky adults belting a radio hit is endearing and comedic
jokes.explanation: The payoff on the road-trip CD setup is functionally sweet more than funny, but the image of Michael and Holly singing together is both character-consistent and comedically warm. Returns later in the episode as a running gag/callback.

jokes.text: Dwight claims Cornell's agricultural program is responsible for modern cabbage: 'Without its agricultural program, we probably wouldn't have cabbage, at least not modern cabbage.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is defending Cornell as an excellent school to demonstrate he knows about it
jokes.punchline: 'At least not modern cabbage' — the qualifier is perfectly absurd; what is 'modern cabbage' as opposed to ancient cabbage?
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'At least not modern cabbage' is a masterclass in absurdist comedy — the qualifier implies there's a meaningful distinction between modern and non-modern cabbage, delivered with total Dwight conviction. It's specific (cabbage = beets adjacent, Dwight's world), confident, and completely unhinged. The phrase 'modern cabbage' alone is highly quotable and bizarre in the best way. Earns 8.5 comfortably.

jokes.text: Dwight says 'Stop saying we' — he keeps referring to Cornell as 'we' despite not being an alumnus or even an applicant yet
jokes.setup: Dwight and Andy debate Cornell football; Dwight keeps using 'we' as if he's a Cornell man
jokes.punchline: Andy has to remind Dwight he did not attend Cornell and is 'just doing this to screw with me'
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the Cornell bit — Dwight has already fully adopted the identity. Andy's exasperated 'stop saying we' is relatable and well-timed. Part of the running Cornell gag that builds throughout.

jokes.text: 'Someday we'll both get together in Comstock Hall and just laugh about all of this.'
jokes.setup: Andy insists Dwight didn't go to Cornell and is just doing this to mess with him
jokes.punchline: Dwight responds with false warmth and an invitation to a specific Cornell dorm — as if they're future alumni together — which is absurd given the adversarial context
jokes.explanation: Dwight's false sentimentality is perfectly placed — he's simultaneously escalating the antagonism and performing camaraderie. The specificity of 'Comstock Hall' makes it funnier than a generic reference.

jokes.text: Pam's talking-head: 'I think they're into the idea. They're probably thinking, "That Pam Beesly, she's the coolest sister-in-law on the planet. She's the best, the absolute best."'
jokes.setup: Pam describes pitching a prank to Jim's brothers, claiming they're excited about it
jokes.punchline: Pam's delusional self-assessment of what the brothers are thinking — 'the absolute best' — clearly not matching the likely reality
jokes.explanation: A mild self-delusion joke in the Michael Scott mode — but from Pam, who is usually self-aware, it signals her nervous need to impress Jim's family. Functional character moment, not a strong standalone joke.

jokes.text: Pam's ring-loss prank idea: she even put makeup on her finger to simulate a ring indent, then calls it 'very subtle'
jokes.setup: Pam explains her elaborate alternative prank — faking losing her engagement ring
jokes.punchline: She reveals she already put makeup on her finger to simulate the tan line, calling it 'very subtle' — it's barely visible, making the preparation hilarious in its commitment
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the over-preparation — Pam already committed to a prank that got replaced, so all that effort was wasted. 'It's very subtle' as self-deprecating acknowledgment that her prop is unconvincing is a nice touch of Pam's dry humor.

jokes.text: Tom immediately tops Pam's prank idea with a crueler, pre-existing one about mocking her for being an artist
jokes.setup: Pam pitches her engagement-ring prank as a collaboration with Jim's brothers
jokes.punchline: The brothers immediately pivot to their OWN prank — one that targets Pam directly — revealing they're not her allies at all
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed misdirect — Pam thought she was orchestrating a prank on Jim; instead, she's accidentally recruited allies for a prank ON HER. The brothers' speed in switching plans reveals exactly the dynamic Jim warned about. Good structural joke that pays off throughout the lunch scene.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, we should totally dog her about being an artist, never making any money... she basically has a hobby for a job.'
jokes.setup: Tom and Pete enthusiastically adopt their own prank idea targeting Pam's career
jokes.punchline: Their casual cruelty ('hobby for a job') delivered with total comfort — this is clearly how they operate
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the brothers' complete comfort with meanness. The cringe comes from Pam standing there as they plan this. Solid cringe setup for the lunch scene.

jokes.text: Holly talking-head: 'This trip is longer than I thought.' Michael: 'Yeah, it did look shorter on the map.'
jokes.setup: They've been driving for a while and are surprised at the distance
jokes.punchline: Michael's explanation — 'it looked shorter on the map' — is the kind of thing only someone who doesn't understand maps or scale would say
jokes.explanation: Mild Michael obliviousness joke. Functional but not particularly inspired.

jokes.text: Michael realizes Holly was asleep and talking in her sleep; Holly says 'Was I saying anything interesting?' / 'Not really.'
jokes.setup: Michael says Holly was talking; Holly asks if she said anything interesting
jokes.punchline: 'Not really.' — the flat dismissal of what Holly apparently said while unconscious
jokes.explanation: A very small beat — good economy, warm delivery implied, but not a joke that stands on its own particularly well.

jokes.text: 'I want to pull over and find a little bed and breakfast for when we meet in the middle. Emphasis on the bed and the breakfast.'
jokes.setup: Michael suggests finding a midpoint hotel for future visits
jokes.punchline: 'Emphasis on the bed and the breakfast' — Michael adds a winking double entendre about the bed while also being genuinely excited about breakfast
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael — the innuendo is obvious but delivered with his particular brand of self-satisfied cleverness. The breakfast enthusiasm may be equally sincere, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Michael and Holly pull off the highway looking for a B&B and find absolutely nothing — 'There's nothing out here, man.'
jokes.setup: Michael confidently pulls over to find a bed and breakfast in rural Pennsylvania
jokes.punchline: They find a completely empty landscape — Michael had imagined a hotel, a pool, a breakfast place 'with really good bacon'
jokes.explanation: Michael's gap between expectation and reality is a running theme — the specific detail of the pool and 'really good bacon' is funny in its specificity. A mild but pleasant joke.

jokes.text: 'Here we go. Fourth time's the charm.' — Michael restarts 'Life Is a Highway' for the fourth time
jokes.setup: The road-trip CD has been playing; Michael has apparently restarted the same song multiple times
jokes.punchline: 'Fourth time's the charm' — the idiom mangled (it's 'third time's a charm') AND the fact that this is the fourth restart
jokes.explanation: A callback that works both as a running gag (the song keeps restarting) and a Michael-ism (mangling the idiom). The combination of the wrong idiom + the specific number 'fourth' is characteristically Michael. Good economy.

jokes.text: Holly is crying in the car; Michael asks if she has allergies; then asks 'Did Darryl touch you?'
jokes.setup: Holly is visibly crying; Michael tries to identify the cause
jokes.punchline: 'Did Darryl touch you?' — a completely random, left-field accusation against Darryl (the warehouse foreman driving) that makes no contextual sense
jokes.explanation: A genuinely excellent joke. Michael cycles through 'allergies?' (a reasonable if oblivious guess) and then leaps to 'Did Darryl touch you?' — an accusation against a specific person (Darryl) who is presumably driving and has done nothing. The jump is so non-sequitur and yet so Michael — he's looking for someone to blame, picks the nearest person, and frames it with genuine concern. Highly quotable, perfectly timed, earned entirely through Michael's character logic. Easily an 8+ joke.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I've dated almost four women in the last...' / Holly: 'I dated four guys last year, too.' / Michael: 'Not last... No, in like the last 10 years I've dated almost four women'
jokes.setup: Michael tries to explain how special Holly is relative to his dating history
jokes.punchline: He's dated 'almost four women' in TEN YEARS — the 'almost' making it funnier — while Holly casually dated four guys in one year; Michael has to correct the misunderstanding, which only makes his romantic history more embarrassing
jokes.explanation: The word 'almost' carrying so much weight — Michael has dated ALMOST four women in 10 years, which means fewer than four — is perfectly constructed. The correction scene where Michael has to clarify makes it worse for him, not better. Strong character comedy with good structure.

jokes.text: Holly: 'Don't make it harder than it has to be.' / Michael: 'That's what she said.'
jokes.setup: Holly is in an emotional moment trying to break things off with Michael; she says 'don't make it harder than it has to be'
jokes.punchline: Michael, even in a moment of genuine heartbreak, cannot resist the 'that's what she said' reflex — but then he immediately follows it with 'I'm going to make this way harder than it needs to be'
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional use of a running gag. The 'that's what she said' comes in the most emotionally raw moment in the episode, which normally would kill a comedy beat — but Michael saying it reflexively (he CANNOT help himself even now) AND then immediately pivoting to mean it sincerely ('I'm going to make this way harder than it needs to be') is a stunning piece of character writing. The joke, the heart, and the character are all in one beat. Earns 8+ confidently.

jokes.text: 'It's pronounced Colonel. It's the highest rank in the military.' / 'It's pronounced Cornell. It's the highest rank in the Ivy League.'
jokes.setup: Someone makes a comment about dating 'guys from Cornell'; Andy sarcastically doubts Cornell would date her
jokes.punchline: Someone mispronounces Cornell as 'Colonel' (the military rank); Andy corrects it by mirroring the structure — 'the highest rank in the Ivy League'
jokes.explanation: An excellent wordplay exchange. The parallel structure ('highest rank in the military' / 'highest rank in the Ivy League') is perfectly matched, and Andy's comeback is both absurdly pretentious and structurally airtight. The absurdity of treating an Ivy League as having 'ranks' the way the military does is the comedic core. Clean, quotable, well-constructed. Earns 8.

jokes.text: Kevin or Meredith says they once dated guys from Cornell who 'gave them a ride home'; Andy says 'I seriously doubt that anyone from Cornell dated you'
jokes.setup: A female coworker claims to have dated Cornell men
jokes.punchline: Andy is so protective of Cornell's reputation that he disputes whether Cornell men would have dated this coworker — an elitist and slightly cruel dismissal
jokes.explanation: Good character joke for Andy — his Cornell snobbery overrides basic social decency. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: 'That's Big Red Bear. That's a bobble Big Red Bear. God!'
jokes.setup: Someone (presumably Dwight) has brought Cornell paraphernalia — a Big Red Bear bobblehead — into the office to torment Andy
jokes.punchline: Andy's outrage escalates to identifying it specifically as a 'bobble Big Red Bear' and reacting with genuine anguish ('God!')
jokes.explanation: Andy's Cornell identity crisis running gag continues. The specific identification of 'bobble Big Red Bear' is funny in its precision — Andy knows EXACTLY what it is, which means it has a name in his world. The 'God!' is a nice escalation.

jokes.text: Michael's plan to stay connected: 'I'll talk to you on the Bluetooth the entire trip... I'll tell you everything I see, everything that I pass by, things that I witness on the road. Maybe I'll see an accident one weekend.'
jokes.setup: Michael proposes a solution to the long-distance problem — constant Bluetooth narration of his drive
jokes.punchline: 'Maybe I'll see an accident one weekend' — Michael treats witnessing a traffic accident as a potential highlight of their long-distance Bluetooth relationship
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever joke. Michael is earnestly trying to make long distance work, offering to narrate his commute — and then his mind goes to 'maybe I'll see an accident,' which he offers as a potential perk of the arrangement. The dark casualness of treating a car crash as entertaining content for Holly is completely Michael. Earns 8.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Here's my wish: I want you to meet a great guy and I want you to be happy.' / Holly: 'Thank you.' / Michael: 'My wish has come true, incidentally, because you've met me and you are happy.'
jokes.setup: Michael appears to have a genuine, selfless moment — wishing for Holly to find happiness
jokes.punchline: Immediately subverts it by pointing out he fulfills both criteria — he IS the great guy, she IS happy — so his wish has already been granted
jokes.explanation: Excellent Michael joke. He fakes selflessness for exactly one sentence before turning it into self-aggrandizement. The structure is perfect — the 'thank you' from Holly makes the punchline land harder. 'Incidentally' is doing wonderful comic work as a transitional word. Holly's 'Clever, Mike' response is the ideal button. Earns 8.

jokes.text: Tom at lunch: 'So, Pam, how much money does an artist make after they leave art school?'
jokes.setup: The lunch begins; Jim is relaxed and Pam knows what's coming but Jim doesn't
jokes.punchline: Tom fires the opening shot of the prank — a pointed career question designed to embarrass Pam
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the brothers' prank plan. Cringe comedy that works because the audience knows the prank setup — Tom's fake innocence is transparent to us but not Jim.

jokes.text: 'Maybe Pam should pay the check by drawing a picture on this napkin.'
jokes.setup: The brothers are escalating their mockery of Pam's art career
jokes.punchline: Pete suggests Pam pay for the meal with napkin art — a cruel but funny escalation of the 'art doesn't pay' theme
jokes.explanation: A sharp line in the cringe comedy sequence. The specificity of 'drawing a picture on this napkin' makes it vivid and mean-funny. Jim's reaction ('Wow, that's a little rude') is the appropriate button.

jokes.text: Michael leaves increasingly desperate voicemails: 'I'm not going to be okay. Please... I'm not strong. I'll go back to Jan, and I hate Jan.'
jokes.setup: Michael, after the near-breakup conversation, calls someone (presumably Ryan or a friend) for support
jokes.punchline: 'I'll go back to Jan, and I hate Jan.' — the specific threat of his own weakness, acknowledging Jan is his self-destructive fallback
jokes.explanation: Rich character comedy. Michael's self-awareness about Jan — 'I hate Jan' while also admitting he'll return to her — is both sad and funny. The escalating desperation of the voicemail is vintage Michael Scott. 'I hate Jan' is a great button.

jokes.text: Dwight interrupts a tense Andy moment with: 'Andy, I've been meaning to ask you. Which a cappella group should I join? The Harmoniacs? Or the Do-Re-Migos?'
jokes.setup: Andy is in the middle of something tense; Dwight derails it with a completely performative Cornell question
jokes.punchline: 'The Do-Re-Migos' is an invented Cornell a cappella group name — the name itself is funny, and Dwight's deadpan sincerity in asking for guidance is perfect
jokes.explanation: The 'Do-Re-Migos' alone is a very funny invented name — it's specific enough to sound real, musical enough to fit a cappella, and slightly wrong in a Dwight-researched way. His framing it as something he's 'been meaning to ask' implies he's been holding this question in reserve, which is a great character beat.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking-head on Andy's Cornell interview: 'If I had to put Dwight's chances into a percentage, I would say he has none percent chance.'
jokes.setup: Andy is conducting Dwight's Cornell admissions interview
jokes.punchline: 'None percent' — not zero percent, but 'none percent' — Andy's specific phrasing betraying both his contempt and his slightly imprecise language
jokes.explanation: 'None percent' is a nice small character-specific word choice — Andy is confident but slightly off-register. Good economy, solid talking-head joke.

jokes.text: Dwight's role models in the Cornell interview: 'Dane Cook, Jack Bauer and Eli Whitney.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks Dwight who his role models are in the formal interview
jokes.punchline: The list: Dane Cook (a comedian known for bro-appeal), Jack Bauer (a fictional TV character), and Eli Whitney (inventor of the cotton gin) — a bizarre mix of low, fictional, and legitimate
jokes.explanation: An excellent Dwight joke. The list's incongruity is the engine — a middlebrow stand-up comedian, a fictional federal agent, and an 18th-century inventor. Each choice is recognizably Dwight: pop-culture validation (Dane Cook), action-heroism (Jack Bauer), and practical American invention (Eli Whitney). The list reveals his entire personality while being genuinely funny. The word 'Jack Bauer' as a role model for a Cornell interview is particularly absurd. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Andy announces the time of the interview in archaic English: 'When the hour glass strikes 3:00, then in the room whence employees confer.' / Dwight: 'What?' / Andy: 'The conference room.'
jokes.setup: Andy is setting up Dwight's interview with exaggerated gravitas
jokes.punchline: He delivers the location in absurd faux-medieval language ('whence employees confer'), then immediately deflates it: 'The conference room'
jokes.explanation: The contrast between Andy's overblown announcement and the mundane reality ('The conference room') is a tight structure. 'Whence employees confer' is a beautiful piece of Andy pomposity. The deflation is well-timed.

jokes.text: Pam defends herself for real mid-prank: 'I mean, it's a very competitive field, but I have a professor who says I have a lot of promise, and if I don't try now, I never will, so...'
jokes.setup: Pam is supposed to be staying in character for the prank — letting Jim's brothers mock her art career
jokes.punchline: She breaks and starts genuinely defending herself mid-prank, revealing real vulnerability — the prank worked too well on her
jokes.explanation: Emotionally rich joke that works on multiple levels. Pam breaks the prank by defending herself for real — the joke being that the brothers hit on a genuine insecurity she didn't expect to be exposed. The 'so...' trailing off is heartbreaking and funny simultaneously. This is The Office at its best: comedy that is also real. High character integration and earned score.

jokes.text: Tom and Pete reveal the prank: 'We pranked you. It was Pam's idea. Pam was the mastermind.'
jokes.setup: Jim has been getting increasingly defensive on Pam's behalf throughout lunch
jokes.punchline: The brothers reveal it was a prank — and immediately throw Pam under the bus by crediting her as 'the mastermind,' which is technically accurate
jokes.explanation: A satisfying payoff to the double-prank setup. The brothers immediately blaming Pam while calling her 'the mastermind' is a small cruelty that's also accurate — and the prank having gone way further than Pam intended is the core joke.

jokes.text: Cornell interview: Dwight answers Cornell history question incorrectly; Andy misidentifies the answer himself in correcting Dwight
jokes.setup: Andy asks a Cornell trivia question ('Who was Cornell's eighth president?') to trip up Dwight
jokes.punchline: Dwight gets it wrong — but Andy's 'correct' answer is actually the SEVENTH president, not the eighth, so Andy is wrong about which question he's asking
jokes.explanation: A layered joke requiring attention. Andy sets a trap for Dwight with Cornell trivia — but Andy himself confused the seventh and eighth presidents, meaning the only person who failed the quiz was the one administering it. The irony of Andy's Cornell pride being undermined by his own imprecise knowledge is excellent character work.

jokes.text: Dwight and Andy's mutual interview evaluation escalation: 'Comprehension skills subpar' / 'Interviewing skills subpar' / 'Applicant is attempting to blackmail interviewer' / 'Interviewer has suspect motives' / 'Applicant has a head shaped like a trapezoid.'
jokes.setup: Dwight starts taking notes on Andy during his own interview; Andy objects and starts writing about Dwight
jokes.punchline: The mutual evaluation escalates to absurd personal attacks — ending with 'Applicant has a head shaped like a trapezoid,' which is both petty and geometrically specific
jokes.explanation: One of the best sequences in the episode. The escalation from professional critique to petty insult is perfectly paced, and 'head shaped like a trapezoid' is a geometrically precise insult that could only come from Dwight — who thinks in agricultural and scientific terms. The mutual simultaneous evaluation is a great structural bit. 'Trapezoid' alone is quotable. Strong 8.5.

jokes.text: 'Interviewer has turned off applicant's interest in Cornell and they are going to go to the vastly superior Dartmouth. Ever heard of it?'
jokes.setup: Dwight's mutual evaluation continues; he escalates to threatening to attend a rival Ivy League
jokes.punchline: 'Ever heard of it?' — Dwight asks if Andy has heard of Dartmouth, an Ivy League that Andy certainly knows, as if it's an obscure institution
jokes.explanation: Dwight asking if Andy — a Cornell man, so certainly Ivy League-aware — has heard of Dartmouth is deliciously condescending and absurd. The 'ever heard of it?' tag is a perfect button to the escalation sequence.

jokes.text: Michael is taking only a lamp from Holly's apartment — Darryl points out there's another dolly in the truck
jokes.setup: Michael is helping Holly move; Darryl notices Michael is only taking a single lamp
jokes.punchline: Michael's impracticality (and denial) is implicit — he's physically undercommitting to the move because emotionally he's not ready to commit to it being real
jokes.explanation: A visual comedy beat that's more poignant than laugh-out-loud funny. The lamp as a symbol of Michael's emotional state works better as character drama than pure comedy.

jokes.text: Jim reading a text from his brother: 'Pam cool. Welcome to the family.'
jokes.setup: Jim reads the verdict text from his brother after the lunch
jokes.punchline: 'Pam cool.' — the brevity and minimalism of the approval text from the guy who just spent lunch roasting her; the terse brotherly communication style
jokes.explanation: The economy is exceptional — 'Pam cool. Welcome to the family.' says everything about the brothers' character, their communication style, and the resolution of the episode's Jim/Pam subplot in six words. The contrast with their elaborate lunch cruelty is the joke. Highly quotable in context.

jokes.text: 'Hey, how about at Thanksgiving we prank Tom about being bald?'
jokes.setup: Pam is relieved the brothers approved of her; she immediately starts plotting revenge
jokes.punchline: Pam immediately plans a retaliatory prank targeting Tom's baldness — revealing she has a streak of competitiveness underneath her warmth
jokes.explanation: A good character beat for Pam — her immediate pivot to revenge is funny and reveals she's more like the Halperts than she realizes. The specificity of 'being bald' as a target is both mean and funny.

jokes.text: Holly decides to ride back with Darryl instead of staying — Michael has to put her things back in the truck
jokes.setup: Michael has carried up a single lamp; Holly decides she's going back
jokes.punchline: Michael has to put the lamp back in the truck — the comedic futility of having carried only a lamp up and now carrying it back down
jokes.explanation: The callback on the lamp is bittersweet — the futility is real and sad, but the image of Michael carrying one lamp up and then immediately back down is physically funny. More emotional than comedic.

jokes.text: Darryl: 'I know it's hard, Mike. Breakups hurt.' / Michael: 'We didn't break up.' / Darryl: 'Looked like it.'
jokes.setup: Michael insists he and Holly didn't break up as Darryl drives him home
jokes.punchline: 'Looked like it.' — Darryl's flat, unimpressed assessment cuts through Michael's denial
jokes.explanation: Darryl's two-word deflation is a perfect straight-man beat. 'Looked like it' is efficient, kind in its honesty, and completely Darryl. Good economy.

jokes.text: Darryl teaches Michael to sing the blues; Michael waits too long, misses his cue, plays harmonica at wrong time
jokes.setup: Darryl offers to teach Michael to sing the blues to cheer him up; explains Michael should hit him with 'what's getting you down' after Darryl's blues line
jokes.punchline: Michael completely fails to follow the simple blues structure — either missing the cue entirely or playing harmonica at the wrong time
jokes.explanation: A physical/musical comedy sequence that's visually rich even in transcript form. Michael's inability to follow the most basic blues call-and-response structure despite genuinely wanting to participate is perfect Michael. Darryl's patient instruction followed by Michael's complete failure is a classic dynamic. The ending 'Never mind' from Darryl is a devastating underreaction.

jokes.text: 'Never mind.' — Darryl gives up on teaching Michael the blues
jokes.setup: Michael has failed to follow the blues instruction correctly; Darryl gives one final attempt
jokes.punchline: 'Never mind.' — Darryl abandons the lesson entirely with two words
jokes.explanation: Darryl's 'never mind' is the perfect two-word button to the blues sequence — maximum economy, perfect Darryl deadpan, and the implication that Michael's failure was so total that continuing is pointless. A great straight-man beat.

jokes.text: Dwight arrives the next morning in the Cornell sweatshirt again: 'Well, I thought I'd come in casual today. Man, hungry. Anyone else feel like a beet?'
jokes.setup: Dwight continues his Cornell torment of Andy into the next day
jokes.punchline: 'Anyone else feel like a beet?' — Dwight pivots to beet promotion while wearing Cornell gear, connecting his two identities (beet farmer and Cornell aspirant)
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'casual today' is a good running gag button, and 'anyone else feel like a beet?' is classic Dwight — non-sequitur agricultural enthusiasm delivered with complete sincerity. The beets connect to the episode's final visual gag.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Man, hungry. Anyone else feel like a beet?' — casually pulling out beets while dressed as Jim.
jokes.setup: Dwight is dressed as Jim but immediately reverts to his most Dwight characteristic: beet farming.
jokes.punchline: Dwight-as-Jim offering beets to coworkers — Jim's easygoing social gesture executed with Dwight's beet obsession — is a perfect fusion of the two characters' traits.
jokes.explanation: The beet offer is the perfect Dwight-as-Jim joke: the gesture (casual offering to coworkers) is Jim, but the content (raw beets from Bernard Farms) is pure Dwight. The costume performance has broken down — Dwight can't maintain Jim's persona without inserting his own obsessions. Excellent character comedy.

jokes.text: 'You're supposed to cook these, aren't you?' / 'Cornell.' — Dwight eats a raw beet and says only 'Cornell' in response
jokes.setup: Andy realizes Dwight is eating raw beets; asks if they should be cooked
jokes.punchline: 'Cornell.' — Dwight's single-word response to a practical cooking question; he says only the word 'Cornell' as an answer to everything, maximizing its use as psychological warfare while also eating a raw beet like an animal
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the best cold-close gags in the series. Dwight is asked a reasonable practical question about cooking beets, and his only response is 'Cornell.' It's a one-word punchline that serves as: (1) a non-answer to a real question, (2) the culmination of the entire Cornell psychological warfare subplot, (3) a demonstration that Dwight is eating raw beets like a feral human, and (4) an absurdist word used as a complete sentence. The economy is perfect — no word in television is funnier than 'Cornell' in this exact context. The rewatch is even better because you've watched Dwight build to this. Comparable to the best Office cold closes.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I see what you are doing, but I do not know where you are going with this.' / Dwight: 'Well, you will as soon as you visit my new beet farm.'
jokes.setup: Andy is suspicious of Dwight's beet-farming revelation
jokes.punchline: Dwight has purchased a beet farm — announced casually as a new development — and is inviting Andy to visit, still implying some larger scheme
jokes.explanation: The revelation that Dwight has started a beet farm is appropriately absurd and completely in character. Andy's bewildered 'I see what you are doing but I do not know where you are going' is a great line — it captures the audience's feeling exactly. Dwight's invitation to the beet farm is a perfect non-answer.

jokes.text: Dwight eats a raw beet at his desk — 'You're supposed to cook these, aren't you?' / 'Cornell.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is eating raw beets at work and someone questions whether they need to be cooked
jokes.punchline: Dwight's single-word response — 'Cornell' — as if his university application answers all questions about proper food preparation
jokes.explanation: Perfect cold episode button. 'Cornell' as Dwight's all-purpose non-answer — to a question about whether beets should be cooked — is the single most economical joke in the episode. One word closes the entire Cornell arc while advancing the beet farm bit. It's the kind of joke that gets better every time you think about it: Dwight has so thoroughly adopted the Cornell identity that 'Cornell' now functions as his personal brand answer to everything. Economy: 10/10. The best closing joke the episode could have had.

tmdb_overview: Pam is embarrassed when she is the only person at corporate wearing a costume on Halloween. Holly and Michael take the long trip to Nashua after they get some shocking news from corporate. Meanwhile, Dwight torments Andy and tries to get under his skin.
